newsitem.title: UK: Energy, some metals to see upturn in 97 -analysts.
newsitem.headline: Energy, some metals to see upturn in 97 -analysts.

text.p: Forecasts of an upturn in the industrial economies in 1997 promise a better year for commodities, but analysts of the sector say not all of them will benefit much. "The debate is one of magnitude rather than direction," said metals market analyst Nick Moore at stockbrokers Fleming Global Mining Group.
"Translating that into orders is more debatable but I think it will happen. The whole cycle is moving. Now it is bonds and equities, commodities will come back into fashion," he added.

Merrill Lynch's market cycles group forecasts a four-percent growth rate in Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD) countries in 1997, a view supported by the acceleration in G7 broad money aggregates.
Kleinwort Benson economists, however, have downgraded the 1997 growth forecast to 3.8 from four percent, citing the desynchronised nature of OECD economies and a wide spread of growth expectations.
"We were very bullish. One reason for lowering the forecast was surplus inventories in Asia particlarly of electronics have to be worked down," said the company's oil analyst Medhi Varzi.

Also supporting the 1997 growth view is that real short term interest rates have come down in the OECD economies to 4.5 percent on average now from seven percent 18 months ago, according to Merrill Lynch market cycle analyst Bijal Shah.

"A portfolio (for 1997) would be loaded with equities relating to commodities particularly influenced by the industrial cycle -- base metals and energy. The others tend to rely more on supply and demand," said Shah.
Even in base metals growth and energy next year higher prices will diverge, analysts said.
The favourites for a spectacular 1997 are energy, followed by aluminium, nickel and zinc.
Precious metals are seen going sideways and parochial issues and an overall long-term downtrend will limit growth in the soft commodities, analysts said.

As for copper, the accepted flagship of the industrial metals, the aftermath of the Sumitomo affair in which the Japanese corporation lost some $2.6 billion in copper trading and rising stocks and production will mitigate against improved demand moving the price dramatically, analysts said.
"Copper led a charmed life during the recession and has traditionally led the section. Now we have to see the metals individually rather than as a pack," Fleming's Moore said.
"The metals that will do best are keyed into overall demand growth, principally aluminium and nickel. Clearly they do not have so onerous a supply background," Moore added.
"Precious metals including gold always participate in a run in commodities. We will see moves in sympathy if not in tandem," Moore said.
Silver and platinum will be driven by industrial offtake, but Moore said gold was still concerned with official sales and supply from the mines was increasing.
McQuarie Equities Ltd's metals analyst Adam Rowley added zinc to nickel and aluminium as a hot metals tip next year.

"Zinc could do well next year but we need 100,000-150,000 tonnes off (world) stocks then it would look in extremely good shape," he said, adding that that might not happen until the third quarter but the price reaction could begin six months earlier.

McQuarie forecast average prices for nickel next year of $9,000 a tonne versus just over $7,060 now, aluminium at $1,700 ($1,350 currently) and zinc averaging $1,200 in 1997 versus around a current $1,020.

New refined copper capacity coming on stream next year should raise world stocks from around a historically low four weeks consumption now to a "more comfortable but still low" 5-1/2 weeks by end 1997.
"Even so, the stock rise will still dampen the price moves," he said, suggesting a copper price average of $2,050 next year versus a current cash price of $1,980.

Energy markets have already had a good performance in 1996 and low physical stocks against already rising northern hemisphere winter demand showed current high underlying prices were not an aberration, analysts said .
"They could perform again in 1997. We have been advocating an overweight position in the energy sector. There is nothing to suggest a fall in oil prices," saids Varzi.
How things go for oil markets will become clearer in the next couple of months.

"We will know better then whether or not there is to be a mild winter in the northern hemisphere, the Opec November meeting will have decided on export quotes and the U.S. election will be over so it can then focus more on Iraq," Varzi said.
